newsitem.title: UK: A huge speculative play is swinging coffee.
newsitem.headline: A huge speculative play is swinging coffee.

text.p: Speculators who hope for a windfall if frost hits Brazil's crop this year are behind wild gyrations in the world coffee markets that mean millions of drinkers are paying more for a cup of their favourite beverage.

In one of the biggest financial gambles in today's marketplace, big investment funds and smaller speculators bet that frost in Brazil, the leading grower, might worsen an already-tight supply situation.

A tide of "hot" money so far this year has doubled coffee futures - with New York values for quality arabica beans recently at the highest in 20 years - triggering retail price rises in shops around the world.

"The speculation on the commodity market...may have the character of a self-fulfilling prophecy," said Britain's Fairtrade Foundation, a charity that tries to promote ethical trading practices with the Third World.
"It is certain that it is not the coffee growers who benefit from the profits earned from speculation," it said.
This year's bull run has been unprecedented in the sense that there has not actually been a frost in Brazil.

The crunch will come in the next few weeks at the height of winter in Brazil. If there is no frost, a rush to unload "paper" coffee might burst the speculative bubble - which is why some players have already cashed in gains and coffee futures are below their recent peaks.
The rally has been further fuelled by aggressive buying by roasters (processors) as they replenished unusually low stocks.
Speculators who have piled in to coffee before the June-July frost season in Brazil recall how prices quadrupled after frost, then drought. there in 1994.
New York July arabica coffee futures traded this week around $2.50 per pound, down from more than $3 seen last week but about double where they began 1997.
"Should a frost of 1994's magnitude hit Brazilian coffee areas over the next few months, then coffee prices could soar to $5, perhaps $7 per pound," broker GNI Ltd said in a report.
"But if a frost is not seen, the downside for prices could perhaps be $1.50 or so. It seems like a fair bet," it said.

Professor Christopher Gilbert of the University of London's Queen Mary College, who has just published a study of the coffee market between 1993 and 1996, said the chance of a frost this year was slim.
"It happens in one out of seven years," he said. There were severe frosts in 1976 and 1981 as well as 1994.
His study found that the last major coffee boom in 1993/95 netted more than $400 million in profits for speculators, particularly funds.

"Our central estimates show large speculators as having made a second and third quarter 1994 profit on CSCE (the New York arabica coffee futures) of over $600 million and a profit of over $400 million over the entire 1994-95 period," said the study.

"Since small speculators also made money, this implies large losses to hedgers - of the order of $900 million in the second and third quarters of 1994 and $550 million over the entire period," it said.
Speculators were fortunate in having accumulated long positions when the Brazilian frosts hit in June and July 1994, the study added.
But whether the "specs" will strike big this time remains to be seen.
Already, both producers and consumers are bracing for a sharp downward spiral if the specs decide to quit coffee.
Last month, key producers led by Brazil resisted pressure to release more coffee onto the market despite soaring prices for fear of a sharp retracement later in the year.
Growers have long maintained that it was neither in the interest of the users nor the farmers to have boom and bust cyles.
Nestle UK, which raised its coffee prices on Monday, said its upward revision was moderate based on the assumption that coffee bean prices would fall back in the latter part of the year.
